vignette: The first crack in his world appears on a Tuesday in 2009. He is forty-two, standing in his kitchen, when his partner’s fist meets his jaw. The violence unfolds not as a single event but as a pattern that tightens over months, then years. He learns to read the shift in his partner’s breathing, the way a dropped mug precedes a shove, the careful geometry of staying out of reach. He files the fear away behind his ribs, where it hardens like set concrete. His Oceania heritage, once a source of communal warmth, now feels distant; he stops attending church gatherings, convincing himself he is simply tired, when in truth he is conserving the last of his reserves. Work becomes his anchor. He spends his days on scaffolding and job sites across the region, laying foundations, framing roofs, reading the grain of timber and the tension in steel. The physicality of it grounds him. His hands, calloused and lined with grime, measure twice and cut once, a rhythm that promises control. But the rhythm fractures when the phone rings with wrong numbers, when a heavy tool bucket drops, when a colleague’s raised voice sounds like a command. He stops taking night shifts. He begins checking the locks on his doors three times before he leaves for work, his breath catching in his throat, his neck muscles coiled tight. The world feels less like a place to build and more like a site to survive. When his partner dies, the silence he expected does not come. Instead, the house amplifies every sound. He wakes at 3 a.m. staring at the ceiling, his heart hammering against his sternum, certain he hears footsteps in the hall. The grief arrives in waves, but it is tangled with something else—a low-grade alarm that never switches off. He avoids the grocery store where they once argued. He cannot sit with friends at dinner if they raise their hands to emphasize a point. He stops sleeping on his back. He piles pillows against the headboard, facing the door, his hands resting near the floor where his belt hangs. His children, grown and living in other cities, call less often. He watches them from a distance, afraid that leaning in will pull them into the same darkness that claimed his home. Now, at sixty-three, he walks into the consultation room with the same deliberate pace he uses on a job site. He sits on the edge of the chair, his spine straight, his weight forward. His eyes track the exit, the window, the space behind the door. He speaks in measured sentences, his voice steady, but his right thumb rubs a circular groove into his left forefinger. He recounts the community center project he is framing this week. He describes how he now stands at the perimeter of the site, watching the younger crews, his shoulders constantly scanning for threats that aren’t there. When a delivery truck backfires outside, his entire body jolts. He does not swear. He simply exhales slowly, presses his palms flat against his thighs, and waits for the tremor to pass. He carries the weight of years he never unloaded, sitting quietly in the present moment, fully aware of the chair beneath him, the light through the blinds, the quiet hum of the building.
